key_insight: In a hypersonic shock/turbulent boundary-layer interaction, finite-rate chemistry changes the flow more than caloric-property modeling, shrinking the separation bubble and reducing post-shock heating.
engineering_relevance: For hypersonic vehicle design, using a reacting-gas model can materially alter predicted loads and thermal protection requirements, while thermally vs. calorically perfect assumptions are comparatively close.
method: 3 direct numerical simulations of an oblique shock interacting with a turbulent high-enthalpy boundary layer
Identical geometry and freestream conditions with three thermochemical models: finite-rate reactive, thermally perfect, and calorically perfect
Compared separation, wall heat flux, temperature statistics, and reflected-shock inclination
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the reactive case produces a smaller separation bubble, lower mean/fluctuating temperatures and wall heat flux, and a less inclined reflected shock than the simplified gas models.
watch_item: The conclusion is specific to this high-enthalpy Mach 6.4 regime, so the balance between frozen and reacting behavior may differ at other enthalpies or shock strengths.
paper_title: Effects of thermochemical modelling on a hypersonic shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interaction
